title: The Mystery of the Yuba County Five
big_number_label: C-ration cans were eaten, but the locker with a year's worth of food was never opened
takeaways: On February 24, 1978, five friends from Yuba County, California went to watch a basketball game in Chico and never came home.
Their car was found up in the mountains of Plumas National Forest, still running and with gas in the tank. Four of them were later found dead.
Gary Mathias, the fifth, has never been found. The case is still unsolved.

quiz.q: Where was the Yuba County Five's car found?
options: In the Chico State parking lot
Next to their homes in Yuba City

quiz.q: How many C-ration cans were found opened and eaten outside the trailer?
Which of the five has still never been found?

paragraphs: They just went to watch a basketball game. But instead of going home, these five men ended up on a freezing mountain. Four were found dead. The fifth is still missing to this day. Let's meet them.
Jack Madruga, thirty. Bill Sterling, twenty-nine. Jackie Huett, twenty-four.
Ted Weiher, thirty-two. And Gary Mathias, twenty-five. All of them had an intellectual disability or a mental illness. They played together on a basketball team, the Gateway Gators.

Gary was a former soldier who had been diagnosed with schizophrenia and was in treatment at the time. February 24, 1978. They drove to Chico to watch UC Davis play Chico State. Davis won. And the next day, it was their turn: their first game in a Special Olympics tournament. Some of them had already laid out their uniforms. This was the last thing Ted wrote in his notebook.

At around ten that night, they bought snacks, soda, and milk at a store. The clerk remembered them because they held up her closing. That was the last confirmed sighting of them. They never made it home. The next morning, their families reported them to the police. A few days later, a forest ranger said he had seen their car on February 25, up in the mountains of Plumas National Forest. It was about 70 miles from Chico, and far off the road home.

According to Jack's family, he hated the cold and had never been up in the mountains. On February 28, the police went to the car. It was only stuck in the snow. When they hotwired it, it started right away, and it still had a quarter tank of gas. According to the police, five men could have pushed it out of the snow. The keys were missing. It was unlocked, and one window was rolled down, something Jack supposedly would never do. And even though the road was rough, there wasn't a single scratch on the underside of the car.

Inside: snack wrappers, the game program, and a neatly folded map of California. But then a heavy snowstorm hit. The searchers nearly got lost themselves, so the search was called off. Let's go back to the night of February 24. There was a witness: Joseph Schons. His car got stuck on the same road, that same night. He felt symptoms of a heart attack, so he stayed inside his car.

About six hours later, he saw headlights behind him and a group of people. One of them, he said, looked like a woman carrying a baby. He called out for help. But they went quiet, and the lights went out. The next morning, he walked eight miles to a lodge. On the way back, they passed the five men's car, at the very spot where he had heard the voices. There was one more witness. A woman at a store in Brownsville said she saw four of them the next day, riding in a red pickup.

More than three months passed. On June 4, the snow had melted. A group of motorcyclists went into a Forest Service trailer, 19.4 miles from the car. A window was broken. Inside, they found Ted on a bed, wrapped in eight blankets, head included. He died of starvation and hypothermia. He had lost almost half of his two hundred pounds. Judging by the length of his beard, he may have survived for about three more months.

His feet were nearly gangrenous from frostbite. And his shoes were gone. On the table: his wallet, still with money in it, a ring engraved with the name Ted, and a gold watch that, according to his family, wasn't his. The chilling part? Outside, there were thirty-six C-ration cans that had been opened and eaten. But a locker holding a year's worth of food was never opened.

There was gas for the heater, matches, and books that could have been burned for warmth. There were even heavy clothes. But none of it was used. And the cans? They were opened with a P-38, an Army can opener. Of the five, only Gary and Jack knew how to use one. The next day, the remains of Jack Madruga and Bill Sterling were found on opposite sides of the road, 11.4 miles from the car.

Two days later, Jackie Huett's own father found his son's remains, two miles from the trailer. But Gary Mathias? His tennis shoes were in the trailer. He may have put on Ted's shoes and left. His photo was sent to mental institutions all over California. But to this day, he has never been found. The police theory: they may have been heading to Gary's friends in Forbestown and got lost. When the car got stuck, they supposedly followed a snowcat's tracks, hoping to find shelter.

When they reached the trailer, maybe they were afraid to use anything inside, in case they got accused of stealing. But that doesn't explain everything. Who were the people Schons saw? Why did they leave a car that still ran? As the Yuba County undersheriff put it: this case is bizarre as hell. And according to Jack's mother: we know someone made them do it.
